decks.title: Introduction to Euclid's Geometry: Part 1, origins, definitions and axioms
goals: Describe how geometry grew in Egypt, India and Greece
Explain the Sulba Sutra rope rules and the Harappan brick ratio at a simple level
State what Euclid's Elements is and how it is built
Recall Euclid's definitions and five common notions (axioms) and use them in simple proofs

slides.heading: Where geometry began
slides.body_md: The word geometry means measuring the earth. Farmers, builders and priests needed it long before anyone wrote proofs.

rows: Marking field boundaries again after the Nile floods; laying out corners of buildings with knotted ropes
Bricks made in the ratio $4 : 2 : 1$; streets and buildings laid out in neat rectangles
Priests and builders, with Baudhayana as a famous author
Rope rules for building squares, rectangles and altars, including a rule equivalent to the Pythagorean theorem
Thinkers such as Thales, then Euclid, about $300$ BCE
Proving geometric statements step by step from a few assumptions

visual.alt: Table of three places. Egypt: rope-stretchers re-marked fields after the Nile floods. India: Harappan bricks in the ratio 4 to 2 to 1, and the Sulba Sutras with rope rules for altars. Greece: thinkers who proved results, and Euclid about 300 BCE.
visual.caption: Geometry grew from practical needs in many places.

slides.narration: The word geometry means measuring the earth. In Egypt, India and Greece people needed geometry to mark fields after floods, to make bricks and altars, and later to build a whole science of proofs. In this chapter we visit all three places, and then we read the rules that Euclid chose as the foundation of geometry.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Tell the story of geometry in **Egypt**, **India** and **Greece**
Explain the **Sulba Sutra** rope rules and the **brick ratio**
Describe **Euclid's Elements**
Use Euclid's **axioms** in simple proofs

visual.alt: Flow of Part 1: geometry in Egypt, then in India with Harappan bricks and the Sulba Sutras, then in Greece with Euclid, his definitions and his axioms.
visual.caption: Part 1 road map.

slides.narration: In this part we first look at the practical geometry of Egypt and India. Then we move to Greece and to Euclid's Elements. We read his definitions and his five axioms, and we use the axioms in a small proof. In the next part we study his five postulates and make two constructions.

slides.heading: Egypt: the rope-stretchers
slides.body_md: After each flood of the Nile, boundaries of fields had to be marked again. Rope-stretchers are said to have used a rope with knots at equal spaces. A loop of $12$ spaces makes a triangle with sides $3$, $4$, $5$, and the corner between the $3$ and the $4$ is a right angle.

visual.alt: A right-angled triangle with sides of 3, 4 and 5 equal rope spaces, the right angle at A. A loop of rope with 12 equal spaces, knotted at the corners, makes this triangle.
visual.caption: A loop of $12$ equal spaces: sides $3$, $4$, $5$. The right angle is between the sides $3$ and $4$.

slides.narration: After each flood of the river Nile, field boundaries had to be marked again. Rope-stretchers are said to have used a rope with knots at equal spaces. A loop of twelve spaces can be pulled into a triangle with sides three, four and five. The corner between the sides three and four is a right angle, so the builders could mark square corners.

slides.heading: India: bricks of the Harappan cities
slides.body_md: Bricks found at Harappan sites are often in the ratio length : breadth : thickness $= 4 : 2 : 1$. With thickness $t$, the brick is $4t$ long and $2t$ wide. Equal bricks stack neatly in walls.

visual.alt: Three faces of a brick drawn to one scale: the top face is a rectangle 4 units long and 2 wide, the side face is 4 long and 1 thick, and the end face is 2 wide and 1 thick. So length, breadth and thickness are in the ratio 4 to 2 to 1.
visual.caption: A brick with length : breadth : thickness $= 4 : 2 : 1$, seen from the top, the side and the end.

slides.narration: In the Harappan cities of the Indus valley, many bricks were made in the ratio four to two to one for length, breadth and thickness. If the thickness is t, the length is four t and the breadth is two t. Bricks of one fixed shape fit together neatly in walls, drains and platforms.

slides.heading: Quick check: a brick
slides.body_md: A brick with length, breadth and thickness in the ratio four to two to one is thirty-six centimetres long. What is its thickness?

visual.alt: Three faces of a brick drawn to one scale: the top face is a rectangle 4 units long and 2 wide, the side face is 4 long and 1 thick, and the end face is 2 wide and 1 thick. So length, breadth and thickness are in the ratio 4 to 2 to 1.
visual.caption: A brick with length : breadth : thickness $= 4 : 2 : 1$, seen from the top, the side and the end.

slides.narration: The length is four parts. Find one part.

slides.heading: India: the Sulba Sutras
slides.body_md: The **Sulba Sutras** are ancient Indian texts with rules for building altars. _Sulba_ means a cord or rope. Baudhayana is one well-known author. The rules use ropes to make squares, rectangles and circles.

rows: A square drawn on the diagonal of a square has twice its area
The rope along the diagonal makes an area equal to the two areas made by the sides together
Sets of three numbers that fit this rule were known and used

visual.alt: Table of Sulba Sutra ideas: a square on the diagonal has twice the area, with side 10 becoming 10 root 2; the rope along the diagonal of a rectangle gives the sum of the two side areas, so 12 by 5 has diagonal 13; and number triples such as 3, 4, 5 and 5, 12, 13.
visual.caption: Baudhayana, a Sulba Sutra author, states the rope rule for a rectangle.

slides.narration: The Sulba Sutras are ancient Indian texts with rules for building altars. The word sulba means a cord. Builders used ropes and pegs to draw squares, rectangles and circles on the ground. One well-known author is Baudhayana. His rules include a statement equivalent to the Pythagorean theorem for a rectangle and its diagonal.

slides.heading: A square on the diagonal
slides.body_md: A square built on the diagonal of a square has **twice** its area. In the figure the big square has area $16$ and the small one $8$. If the side of an altar is $10$ m, a double-area altar has side $10\sqrt{2}$ m.

visual.alt: A big square ABCD with a smaller square EFGH drawn inside it by joining the mid-points of its sides. The diagonal EG of the small square is a side of the big square, so the big square is built on that diagonal and has twice the area of the small one.
visual.caption: The square $ABCD$ is built on the diagonal $EG$ of the square $EFGH$. Area of $ABCD$ is $16$, area of $EFGH$ is $8$.

math: \text{area on the diagonal} = 2 \times \text{area of the square}
slides.narration: Here is a picture of the rule. Join the mid-points of the sides of the big square to get a smaller square. The diagonal of the small square is a side of the big square. So the big square is built on that diagonal, and its area is twice the small one. Sixteen is twice eight. Altar builders used this to double the area of an altar.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: ratios and ropes
slides.body_md: Use the brick ratio and the rope rule to find these lengths.
bullets: **Brick —** thickness $6$ cm gives length $24$ cm and breadth $12$ cm
**Altar diagonal —** a $12$ m by $5$ m rectangle: $12^2 + 5^2 = 169$, so the rope is $13$ m
**Double area —** a square of side $10$ m has area $100$ square metres; a square of area $200$ has side $10\sqrt{2} \approx 14.14$ m

rows: Brick with thickness $6$ cm: length and breadth
Rectangular altar $12$ m by $5$ m: diagonal rope
Square altar of side $10$ m: side of a square of double area

visual.alt: Table: a brick with thickness 6 centimetres has length 24 and breadth 12; a rectangular altar 12 metres by 5 metres has a diagonal rope of 13 metres; a square altar of side 10 metres needs a side of 10 root 2, about 14.14 metres, for double the area.
visual.caption: Ratios and the rope rule give lengths directly.

slides.narration: For the brick, multiply the thickness six by four for the length and by two for the breadth. For the rectangular altar, add the squares of the two sides, which gives one hundred sixty-nine. The rope along the diagonal is thirteen metres. For double the area, the new side is the diagonal of the old square, about fourteen point one four metres.

slides.heading: Approximations in the Sulba Sutras
slides.body_md: A Sulba rule for $\sqrt{2}$ is $1 + \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3 \times 4} - \dfrac{1}{3 \times 4 \times 34}$, which gives $\dfrac{577}{408} \approx 1.414216$. It differs from the true value by less than $0.000003$. There are also rope rules to turn a square into a circle of nearly equal area.

visual.alt: Table of the Sulba Sutra rule for the square root of 2: starting from 1, add one third, add one twelfth, then take away one four hundred eighth. The value is about 1.414216, very close to the calculator value 1.414214.
visual.caption: A Sulba rule for $\sqrt{2}$ is correct to five decimal places.

slides.narration: The Sulba Sutras also give clever approximations. One rule for the square root of two starts with one, adds one third, adds one twelfth, and then takes away one part in four hundred eight. The result is very close to the calculator value. Other rules use ropes to turn a square into a circle of nearly the same area.

slides.body_md: The Sulba Sutras are best described as ancient Indian texts that give

The rope along the diagonal makes an area equal to the two areas made by the sides together
Sets of three numbers that fit this rule were known and used

visual.alt: Table of Sulba Sutra ideas: a square on the diagonal has twice the area, with side 10 becoming 10 root 2; the rope along the diagonal of a rectangle gives the sum of the two side areas, so 12 by 5 has diagonal 13; and number triples such as 3, 4, 5 and 5, 12, 13.
visual.caption: Baudhayana, a Sulba Sutra author, states the rope rule for a rectangle.

slides.heading: Greece: Euclid's Elements
slides.body_md: Greek thinkers wanted to **prove** statements, not only measure. Euclid, in about $300$ BCE, collected the geometry of his time in a book of $13$ chapters called the **Elements**. It starts from a few assumptions and proves everything else from them.

visual.alt: Flow chart of the Elements: first the definitions of terms, then five common notions and five postulates that are accepted without proof, and from them the theorems, which are proved.
visual.caption: Euclid builds geometry from a few assumptions to many proved results.

slides.narration: Greek thinkers wanted to prove that a statement is true, not only to measure. About three hundred years before the common era, Euclid wrote the Elements, a book of thirteen chapters. He began with definitions, then listed a few statements to be accepted without proof, and from these he proved many theorems step by step. This method is still the model for mathematics.

slides.heading: Euclid's definitions
slides.body_md: Euclid began by defining terms. Some of his definitions use words that need defining themselves, so today we leave **point**, **line** and **plane** as **undefined terms** and build the rest from them.

rows: It marks a position and has no size
It has length but no width
A segment has two end points
It has only length and breadth
A flat sheet has two measures
The boundary of a sheet is made of lines

visual.alt: Table of Euclid definitions in simple words: a point has no part, a line has length without breadth, the ends of a line are points, a surface has only length and breadth, and the edges of a surface are lines.
visual.caption: Today point, line and plane are left undefined; Euclid tried to define them.

slides.narration: Euclid began with definitions. A point has no part. A line has length without breadth. The ends of a line are points. But words like part and breadth also need explaining, and this could go on for ever. So today we leave point, line and plane as undefined terms and define everything else using them.

slides.heading: Axioms: the common notions
slides.body_md: Euclid used five **common notions**, which we call **axioms**: general truths about equal things and wholes, true in all of mathematics. Some versions of the Elements list a few more.

rows: Things that are equal to the same thing are equal to one another.
If equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal.
If equals are taken from equals, the remainders are equal.
Things that coincide with one another are equal to one another.
Two segments that fit exactly on each other are equal
The whole is greater than the part.
A whole segment $AB$ is longer than its part $AC$

visual.alt: Table of five common notions: things equal to the same thing are equal to each other; equals added to equals give equals; equals taken from equals give equals; things that coincide are equal; the whole is greater than the part. Each has a short example.
visual.caption: These are general truths, used in all of mathematics.

slides.narration: Euclid listed five common notions, which we call axioms. Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another. Equals added to equals give equals. Equals taken from equals give equals. Things that coincide are equal. And the whole is greater than the part. They are general truths, and they are used in every part of mathematics.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: using a common notion
slides.body_md: Points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ lie in order on a line, with $AB = CD$. Show that $AC = BD$. Take $AB = CD = 2$ and $BC = 3$ to check.
bullets: **Given —** $AB = CD$
**Add $BC$ to both —** $AB + BC = CD + BC$ (equals added to equals)
**Conclude —** $AC = BD$; in numbers $5 = 5$

visual.alt: Four points A, B, C and D in order on a line, with AB and CD marked equal. Adding BC to each of the equal segments AB and CD gives AC equal to BD.
visual.caption: $AB = CD$. Add $BC$ to both: $AC = BD$.

slides.narration: Four points A, B, C and D lie in order on a line, and the segments A B and C D are equal. We add the segment B C to both of them. By the second common notion, equals added to equals give equals. The whole A C is A B plus B C, and the whole B D is B C plus C D. So A C equals B D.

slides.body_md: If x equals y and y equals z, which common notion shows that x equals z?

visual.caption: These are general truths, used in all of mathematics.

slides.narration: Look for the one about things equal to the same thing.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Geometry grew from **practical needs**: Egypt (rope-stretchers), India (Harappan bricks $4 : 2 : 1$, Sulba Sutras), Greece (proof)
Sulba Sutras: rope rules, the diagonal rule for a rectangle, double-area squares, approximations
Euclid's **Elements** (about $300$ BCE): $13$ chapters, built from assumptions
Euclid's **five common notions** (axioms) are general truths about equal things

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: practical needs led to ratios and rope rules in Egypt and India, and then to Euclid, who proved results from a few assumptions.
visual.caption: From practice to proof.

slides.narration: To sum up. Geometry began with practical needs in Egypt and India: rope-stretchers, Harappan bricks and the Sulba Sutra rope rules. In Greece, Euclid built geometry from a few assumptions in the Elements. He gave definitions and five common notions, which we call axioms. In the next part we meet his five postulates.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **History questions (1–2 marks):** name the place, the people and the idea
**Axiom questions (1–2 marks):** quote the common notion that is used
**Proofs (2–3 marks):** state the given, then give a reason for each step
**Mistake:** calling a common notion a postulate
**Mistake:** giving exact dates for old texts when the question does not ask
slides.narration: In history questions, name the place, the people and the idea. In axiom questions, quote the common notion you use. In a short proof, state what is given and write a reason for every step. Two common slips: calling a common notion a postulate, and giving exact dates for old texts that nobody knows exactly.

decks.title: Introduction to Euclid's Geometry: Part 2, postulates and constructions
goals: State Euclid's five postulates and explain why the fifth is special
Distinguish definitions, axioms, postulates and theorems
Construct an equilateral triangle and a square on a segment and justify each step by a postulate

slides.heading: Euclid's five postulates
slides.body_md: A **postulate** is an assumption about geometric figures. Euclid used five. Four are about drawing and angles, and the fifth is about when lines meet.

rows: A straight line can be drawn from any one point to any other point.
Join two points with a ruler
A line segment can be extended as far as we like in a straight line.
A circle can be drawn with any point as centre and any length as radius.
Draw a circle with the compass
All right angles are equal to one another.
If a line crossing two lines makes the interior angles on one side add up to less than two right angles, the two lines meet on that side when extended.

visual.alt: Table of Euclid five postulates in simple words: a line can be drawn between any two points; a segment can be extended; a circle can be drawn with any centre and radius; all right angles are equal; and the fifth, about interior angles adding to less than two right angles, tells us when two lines meet.
visual.caption: Postulates are assumptions about geometric figures.

slides.narration: Euclid listed five postulates. These are assumptions about geometric figures that we accept without proof. The first three tell us what we may draw: a line between two points, an extended segment and a circle. The fourth is about right angles, and the fifth tells us when two lines will meet.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: State all **five postulates**
Say why the **fifth** is special, and state **Playfair's axiom**
Tell a **definition**, **axiom**, **postulate** and **theorem** apart
Give a postulate as the **reason** for each construction step

visual.alt: Flow of Part 2: the five postulates, why the fifth is special, the difference between definition, axiom, postulate and theorem, and two constructions justified by postulates.
visual.caption: Part 2 road map.

slides.narration: In this part we state the five postulates and ask why the fifth is special. We learn to tell a definition, an axiom, a postulate and a theorem apart. Finally we do two constructions, an equilateral triangle and a square, and give a reason from the postulates for every step.

slides.heading: Postulates 1, 2 and 3: what we may draw
slides.body_md: **Postulate 1:** join any two points by a line. **Postulate 2:** extend a segment as far as we like. **Postulate 3:** draw a circle with any centre and any radius. In the figure the circle has centre $A$ and radius $AB$.

visual.alt: A circle with centre A. A segment AB is a radius, the segment AC joins A to another point C on the circle, and the dashed piece BE shows the segment AB being extended beyond B.
visual.caption: Postulate $1$: join $A$ to $C$. Postulate $2$: extend $AB$ to $E$. Postulate $3$: the circle with centre $A$ and radius $AB$.

slides.narration: The first three postulates describe what the ruler and compass can do. Postulate one lets us join any two points, like A and C. Postulate two lets us extend a segment as far as we like, like extending A B to E. Postulate three lets us draw a circle with any centre and any radius, like the circle with centre A and radius A B.

slides.heading: The fifth postulate in a picture
slides.body_md: Postulate 4: all right angles are equal. **Postulate 5:** if a line meets two lines so that the interior angles on one side add up to **less than** $180^\circ$ (two right angles), the two lines meet on that side. Here $70^\circ + 80^\circ = 150^\circ$, so they meet at $P$.

visual.alt: A line t crosses two other lines at U and L. On the right of t the two interior angles are 70 degrees and 80 degrees, which add up to 150 degrees, less than 180 degrees. The two lines lean towards each other and meet at the point P on the right.
visual.caption: Interior angles on one side: $70^\circ + 80^\circ = 150^\circ < 180^\circ$, so the lines meet at $P$ on that side.

slides.narration: The fourth postulate says that all right angles are equal. Now the fifth. A line crosses two other lines, and on the right the interior angles are seventy degrees and eighty degrees. Together they make one hundred fifty degrees, which is less than one hundred eighty. The postulate says the two lines lean towards each other and meet on that side.

slides.heading: Why is the fifth postulate special?
slides.body_md: It is **long and complicated**, unlike the other four. Euclid avoided using it until his $29$th proposition. For about two thousand years mathematicians tried to prove it from the other four, and could not. Later it was shown that it cannot be proved that way, and geometries exist in which it does not hold.

rows: Euclid avoided it until his $29$th proposition
No one tried to remove them
Many mathematicians tried to prove it from the other four

visual.alt: Table comparing postulates 1 to 4 with postulate 5. The first four are short and simple. The fifth is long, was avoided by Euclid until his 29th proposition, and many mathematicians tried to prove it from the others. An equivalent form is Playfair axiom.
visual.caption: The fifth postulate looks more like a theorem than a postulate.

slides.narration: The fifth postulate is long and complicated, unlike the other four. Euclid used it as late as his twenty-ninth proposition. For about two thousand years mathematicians tried to prove it from the other postulates, and failed. Later it was understood that it cannot be proved from them, and that other geometries exist in which it is not true.

slides.heading: Quick check: which postulate?
slides.body_md: Euclid draws a circle with centre $A$ and radius $AB$. Which postulate allows this?

visual.alt: A circle with centre A. A segment AB is a radius, the segment AC joins A to another point C on the circle, and the dashed piece BE shows the segment AB being extended beyond B.
visual.caption: Postulate $1$: join $A$ to $C$. Postulate $2$: extend $AB$ to $E$. Postulate $3$: the circle with centre $A$ and radius $AB$.

slides.narration: Think about which postulate is about circles.

slides.heading: Playfair's axiom
slides.body_md: **Playfair's axiom:** for every line $l$ and every point $P$ not on $l$, there is **exactly one** line through $P$ parallel to $l$. It is equivalent to Euclid's fifth postulate, so many books use it instead.

visual.alt: A horizontal line l and a point P above it. The horizontal line m through P is parallel to l and never meets it. The dashed slanted line through P cuts l at Q, so it is not parallel to l.
visual.caption: Through $P$ there is exactly one line $m$ parallel to $l$. Every other line through $P$, such as $PQ$, meets $l$.

math: \text{through } P \notin l \text{: exactly one line parallel to } l
slides.narration: A simpler way to say the fifth postulate was given by the Scottish mathematician John Playfair. For every line and every point not on it, there is exactly one line through the point that is parallel to the given line. Every other line through the point must cut the given line. This is equivalent to the fifth postulate, so books often use it instead.

slides.heading: Definition, axiom, postulate, theorem
slides.body_md: A **definition** explains a word. An **axiom** and a **postulate** are assumed without proof; Euclid used axiom for general truths and postulate for geometry. A **theorem** is **proved**.

rows: A circle is the set of all points at one distance from a point
A general assumption about equals and wholes, used in all of mathematics
The whole is greater than the part
A circle can be drawn with any centre and radius
A statement that is **proved** from earlier statements
Euclid's Proposition $1$ about the equilateral triangle

visual.alt: Table of four words: a definition tells what a word means; an axiom is a general assumption used in all mathematics; a postulate is an assumption about geometry; a theorem is a statement that is proved. Each has an example.
visual.caption: Today the words axiom and postulate are often used for the same thing.

slides.narration: A definition tells us what a word means. An axiom is a general truth that we assume, like the whole is greater than the part. A postulate is an assumption about geometry, like drawing a circle with any centre and radius. A theorem is different: it is proved from definitions, axioms, postulates and earlier theorems.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: sort the statements
slides.body_md: Decide whether each statement is a definition, an axiom, a postulate or a theorem.
bullets: **A point has no part —** a definition, it explains a word
**Things equal to the same thing are equal —** an axiom, a general truth
**A segment can be extended as far as we like —** a postulate, about figures
**An equilateral triangle can be drawn on any segment —** a theorem, it is proved

rows: It explains the meaning of a word
Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another
A line segment can be extended as far as we like
It is about figures, and it is assumed
An equilateral triangle can be drawn on any given segment
It is proved from postulates and axioms

visual.alt: Table sorting four statements: a point has no part is a definition; things equal to the same thing are equal is an axiom; a segment can be extended is a postulate; an equilateral triangle can be drawn on any segment is a theorem, because it is proved.
visual.caption: Ask: is it explaining a word, assumed, or proved?

slides.narration: Ask one question for each statement: is it explaining a word, is it assumed, or is it proved? A point has no part explains a word, so it is a definition. Things equal to the same thing are equal is a general assumption, an axiom. Extending a segment is a postulate. The last one is proved from the postulates, so it is a theorem.

slides.heading: Quick check: parallel lines
slides.body_md: Through a point not on a line, how many lines parallel to the line can be drawn?

visual.alt: A horizontal line l and a point P above it. The horizontal line m through P is parallel to l and never meets it. The dashed slanted line through P cuts l at Q, so it is not parallel to l.
visual.caption: Through $P$ there is exactly one line $m$ parallel to $l$. Every other line through $P$, such as $PQ$, meets $l$.

slides.narration: Recall Playfair's axiom.

slides.heading: Euclid's first construction
slides.body_md: **Task:** draw an equilateral triangle on a given segment $AB$. Draw circles with centres $A$ and $B$, both of radius $AB$. They meet at $C$. Join $AC$ and $BC$.

visual.alt: Two circles of the same radius AB, one with centre A and one with centre B. They cross at the point C above the line. The triangle ABC has all three sides marked equal.
visual.caption: Circles with centres $A$ and $B$ and radius $AB$ meet at $C$: $AC = AB = BC$.

slides.narration: Euclid's first proposition is to draw an equilateral triangle on a given segment A B. Draw a circle with centre A and radius A B. Draw another circle with centre B and the same radius. The circles cross at a point C. Join C to A and to B. We now show that the triangle A B C has three equal sides.

slides.heading: Why it works: a reason for every step
slides.body_md: Each step uses a postulate or a fact. Radii of one circle are equal, so $AC = AB$ and $BC = AB$. By common notion $1$, $AC = BC = AB$.

rows: Draw the circle with centre $A$ and radius $AB$
Draw the circle with centre $B$ and radius $AB$
Call a point where the circles cross $C$
The circles meet (read from the figure)
Radii of the same circle are equal (definition of a circle)
Things equal to the same thing are equal (common notion $1$)

visual.alt: Table of the six steps in Euclid first construction: draw a circle at A with radius AB by postulate 3, draw a circle at B with radius AB by postulate 3, mark a crossing point C, join AC and BC by postulate 1, note AC and BC both equal AB because they are radii, and conclude AC, BC and AB are equal by common notion 1.
visual.caption: Each step of the construction has a reason.

slides.narration: Every step has a reason. The two circles come from postulate three. The joins A C and B C come from postulate one. A C is a radius of the first circle, so it equals A B. B C is a radius of the second circle, so it also equals A B. Things equal to the same thing are equal, so all three sides are equal.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: two triangles make a rhombus
slides.body_md: Draw equilateral triangles $ABC$ and $ABD$ on opposite sides of $AB$. Show that $AC = CB = BD = DA$.
bullets: **Circles —** the same two circles meet at $C$ above $AB$ and at $D$ below it
**Radii —** $AC = AB = BC$ and $AD = AB = BD$
**Common notion 1 —** all four sides equal $AB$, so $ACBD$ has four equal sides

visual.alt: Two equilateral triangles ABC and ABD on opposite sides of the segment AB. The four sides AC, CB, BD and DA are all marked equal, so the figure ACBD has four equal sides.
visual.caption: Triangles $ABC$ and $ABD$ share $AB$. Then $AC = CB = BD = DA$.

slides.narration: The same two circles cross at two points, one above A B and one below. Call them C and D. sections.body_md:
**Harappan bricks** are often in the ratio length : breadth : thickness $= 4 : 2 : 1$.

The **Sulba Sutras** (sulba means cord) give rope rules for building altars. Baudhayana is a well-known author. One rule says that the rope along the diagonal of a rectangle makes an area equal to the sum of the areas made by the two sides, which is the Pythagorean theorem in words. Euclid, in about $300$ BCE, wrote the **Elements** in $13$ chapters. It starts from definitions, axioms and postulates, and proves theorems from them. This way of building a subject is called an **axiomatic system**.

sections.heading: 4. Axioms and postulates
sections.body_md:
**Euclid's five common notions (axioms):** (1) things equal to the same thing are equal to one another; (2) equals added to equals are equal; (3) equals taken from equals are equal; (4) things that coincide are equal; (5) the whole is greater than the part.

**Euclid's five postulates:** (1) a line can be drawn between any two points; (2) a segment can be extended; (3) a circle can be drawn with any centre and radius; (4) all right angles are equal; (5) if the interior angles on one side of a transversal add up to less than $180^\circ$, the two lines meet on that side.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *History (1–2 marks):* name the place, the people and the idea; no exact dates.
- *Axioms and postulates (1–2 marks):* state the idea, and the number if asked.
- *Proof (2–3 marks):* state the given and a reason for each step.

**Common mistakes**
1. Calling a common notion a postulate.
2. Forgetting that a theorem must be proved.
3. Leaving out the reason for a construction step.
4. Misreading the fifth postulate: the interior angles must be on the same side of the transversal.

questions.solution_md: The length is $4$ parts, so one part, which is the thickness, is $36 \div 4 = 9$ cm. The breadth is $2 \times 9 = 18$ cm, so $18$ cm is the second option, not the thickness. The value $144$ multiplies by $4$ instead of dividing.

questions.solution_md: The rope rule says the square on the diagonal equals the squares on the two sides together: $9^2 + 40^2 = 81 + 1600 = 1681$. The diagonal is $\sqrt{1681} = 41$ m. The value $49$ adds the sides, $31$ subtracts them, and $1681$ is the area of the square on the diagonal.

questions.stem_md: A gardener in Mysuru lays out a triangular flower bed on a rope segment $AB$ of length $8$ m, using Euclid's Proposition $1$. (d) She draws a second equilateral triangle $ABD$ on the other side of $AB$. Show that $AC = CB = BD = DA$. (e) Find the length of rope needed to go round the figure $ACBD$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Draw the circle with centre $A$ and radius $AB$, and the circle with centre $B$ and radius $AB$ (Postulate $3$). They meet at $C$. Join $AC$ and $BC$ (Postulate $1$).

**(b)** $AC = AB$ (radii of the circle with centre $A$) and $BC = AB$ (radii of the circle with centre $B$). Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another (common notion $1$), so $AC = BC = AB$.

**(c)** Perimeter $= 3 \times 8 = 24$ m.

**(d)** The same circles meet again at $D$ on the other side of $AB$. As in (b), $AD = AB = BD$. So $AC = CB = BD = DA = AB$ (common notion $1$).

**(e)** The rope goes along $AC$, $CB$, $BD$, $DA$: $4 \times 8 = 32$ m.

questions.stem_md: A carpenter in Jaipur makes a square tile with side $AB = 5$ cm by the construction in the Elements. (a) Extend $BA$ beyond $A$ to $B^{\prime}$ with $AB^{\prime} = AB$. Which postulates make this possible? (b) With centres $B$ and $B^{\prime}$ and radius $8$ cm, two circles meet at $X$. Which postulate is used? (c) Join $AX$ and explain why $AX$ is at right angles to $BB^{\prime}$. (d) Mark $D$ on $AX$ with $AD = AB$, and draw circles of radius $AB$ about $B$ and $D$ meeting again at $C$. Why are $BC$ and $DC$ equal to $AB$? (e) Why is $ABCD$ a square? Find its area and its perimeter.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Postulate $2$ extends $BA$ beyond $A$, and Postulate $3$ (circle with centre $A$ and radius $AB$) gives $B^{\prime}$ with $AB^{\prime} = AB$.

**(b)** Postulate $3$: a circle can be drawn with any centre and any radius.

**(c)** $AX$ is drawn by Postulate $1$. Since $XB = XB^{\prime} = 8$ cm and $AB = AB^{\prime}$, the point $A$ is the mid-point of $BB^{\prime}$ and $X$ is equally far from $B$ and $B^{\prime}$, so $AX$ is the perpendicular bisector of $BB^{\prime}$: the angle at $A$ is a right angle.

**(d)** $C$ lies on the circle with centre $B$ and radius $AB$, so $BC = AB$, and on the circle with centre $D$ and radius $AB$, so $DC = AB$. Also $AD = AB$ by the choice of $D$.

**(e)** The four sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$ are all $5$ cm and the angle at $A$ is a right angle, so $ABCD$ is a square. Its area is $5 \times 5 = 25$ square cm and its perimeter is $4 \times 5 = 20$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Postulates 2 and 3, the perpendicular bisector, and radii of equal circles.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Postulate 3 and (c) the right angle at A
(e) four equal sides and a right angle

questions.stem_md: Two straight roads on a hillside are crossed by a third road (a transversal). (a) On the right of the transversal the interior angles are $68^\circ$ and $79^\circ$. Find their sum and say whether the roads meet, and on which side. (b) State Euclid's fifth postulate. (c) For another pair of roads the interior angles on the right are $112^\circ$ and $68^\circ$. Find their sum and say what the fifth postulate tells us. (d) State Playfair's axiom. (e) Give two reasons why the fifth postulate is considered special.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $68^\circ + 79^\circ = 147^\circ$, which is less than $180^\circ$ (two right angles). So the roads meet on the right of the transversal when extended.

**(b)** If a line crosses two lines so that the interior angles on one side add up to less than two right angles, the two lines meet on that side when extended.

**(c)** $112^\circ + 68^\circ = 180^\circ$. The sum is not less than $180^\circ$, so the postulate does not say that the lines meet on the right (they are in fact parallel, which we prove in the next chapter).

**(d)** For every line $l$ and every point $P$ not on $l$, exactly one line through $P$ is parallel to $l$.

**(e)** It is long and complicated compared with the other four postulates, and Euclid avoided using it until his $29$th proposition. Many mathematicians tried for centuries to prove it from the other postulates and could not.

questions.solution_md: Add the interior angles and compare with 180 degrees.

marking_scheme.step: (a) sum 147 degrees, the roads meet on the right

questions.stem_md: A temple builder in Tamil Nadu uses the rope rules of the Sulba Sutras. (a) A rectangular altar is $15$ m by $36$ m. Find the rope along its diagonal. (b) Show that the square on the diagonal has the same area as the squares on the two sides together. (c) A square altar has side $20$ m. A second square altar of double the area is needed. Find its side, correct to two decimal places. (d) A $60$ m rope is knotted so that its parts are in the ratio $5 : 12 : 13$. Find the three parts. (e) Show that the triangle made by this rope has a right angle.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $15^2 + 36^2 = 225 + 1296 = 1521$, so the diagonal is $\sqrt{1521} = 39$ m.

**(b)** The squares on the sides have areas $225$ and $1296$, which total $1521$, and the square on the diagonal has area $39^2 = 1521$. They are equal.

**(c)** The new area is $2 \times 20^2 = 800$ square metres, so the side is $\sqrt{800} = 20\sqrt{2} \approx 28.28$ m (the diagonal of the old square).

**(d)** $5 + 12 + 13 = 30$ parts, so one part is $60 \div 30 = 2$ m. The parts are $10$ m, $24$ m and $26$ m.

**(e)** $10^2 + 24^2 = 100 + 576 = 676 = 26^2$, so the square on the longest side equals the squares on the other two together: the angle between the $10$ m and $24$ m parts is a right angle.

questions.solution_md: Rope rule: square on the diagonal equals the sum of the squares on the sides.

(e) Repeat (c) for $AB = 30$ cm and $AX = BY = 7$ cm.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $AY = AB - BY$ and $BX = AB - AX$.

**(b)** $AB = AB$ (the same segment), and $AX = BY$ (given). Taking equals from equals gives equal remainders (common notion $3$): $AB - BY = AB - AX$, that is, $AY = BX$.

**(c)** $AY = 20 - 6 = 14$ cm and $BX = 20 - 6 = 14$ cm. The middle part $XY = 20 - 6 - 6 = 8$ cm.

**(d)** Common notion $3$ (equals taken from equals are equal), and also common notion $4$ in the sense that the segment $AB$ equals itself.

**(e)** $AY = 30 - 7 = 23$ cm and $BX = 30 - 7 = 23$ cm, and $XY = 30 - 7 - 7 = 16$ cm.

questions.passage_md: A site museum in Gujarat displays a brick of the Harappan type. Its length, breadth and thickness are in the ratio $4 : 2 : 1$, and its length is $28$ cm.

children.stem_md: The breadth of the brick, in centimetres, is
children.solution_md: The length is $4$ parts, so one part is $28 \div 4 = 7$ cm. The breadth is $2 \times 7 = 14$ cm. The value $7$ is the thickness, $56$ is double the length and $28$ is the length.

children.stem_md: Find the volume of the brick in cubic centimetres.
children.solution_md: The dimensions are $28$, $14$ and $7$ cm, so the volume is $28 \times 14 \times 7 = 2744$ cubic centimetres.

children.stem_md: **(i)** A rectangular floor $112$ cm by $56$ cm is covered with these bricks laid flat (the length by breadth face up), without gaps or cuts. How many bricks are needed?

answer.model_answer_md: A flat brick covers $28$ cm by $14$ cm. Along the $112$ cm side there are $112 \div 28 = 4$ bricks, and along the $56$ cm side $56 \div 14 = 4$ bricks, so $4 \times 4 = 16$ bricks are needed.

children.solution_md: Divide each side of the floor by the matching side of a brick.

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** A stack of $15$ of these bricks, laid flat one on top of another, makes a platform. Find the height of the stack.

answer.model_answer_md: Each brick laid flat is $7$ cm thick, so the height is $15 \times 7 = 105$ cm.

alternatives.solution_md: Multiply the thickness by the number of bricks.

questions.passage_md: A land surveyor in Rajasthan copies the rope-stretchers. She takes a $48$ m rope and ties knots so that its three parts are in the ratio $3 : 4 : 5$. She pulls the rope tight into a triangle to mark a corner of a field.

children.stem_md: The sides of the triangle, in metres, are
children.solution_md: The ratio adds up to $3 + 4 + 5 = 12$ parts, so each part is $48 \div 12 = 4$ m and the sides are $12$, $16$, $20$ m. The sides $9$, $12$, $15$ are in the same ratio but add up to $36$, and $10$, $24$, $26$ add up to $60$.

children.stem_md: The triangle has a right angle between its two shorter sides. Find its area in square metres.
children.solution_md: The two shorter sides are $12$ m and $16$ m and meet at the right angle, so the area is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 12 \times 16 = 96$ square metres.

children.stem_md: **(i)** Show, using the rope rule for a rectangle's diagonal, that the corner between the shorter sides is a right angle.

answer.model_answer_md: The squares on the shorter sides are $12^2 = 144$ and $16^2 = 256$, which add up to $400 = 20^2$, the square on the longest side. So the corner between the $12$ m and $16$ m sides is a right angle.

children.solution_md: Compare the sum of the two smaller squares with the square on the longest side.

marking_scheme.step: 400 = 20^2, so the corner is a right angle

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** She now uses a $60$ m rope with parts in the ratio $5 : 12 : 13$. Find the three parts in metres and check that this also gives a right angle.

answer.model_answer_md: $5 + 12 + 13 = 30$ parts, so one part is $60 \div 30 = 2$ m. The parts are $10$, $24$ and $26$ m. Check: $10^2 + 24^2 = 100 + 576 = 676 = 26^2$, so there is a right angle.

alternatives.solution_md: Divide the rope into 30 parts and check the squares.

questions.passage_md: A village in Maharashtra has a square altar of side $8$ m. The priests want a second square altar of exactly double the area, and the builder uses the Sulba Sutra idea of a square built on a diagonal.

children.stem_md: The area of the new altar, in square metres, is
children.solution_md: The old area is $8^2 = 64$ square metres, so double the area is $2 \times 64 = 128$ square metres. The value $64$ is the old area, $16$ is double the side, and $256$ is four times the old area.

children.stem_md: Find the side of the new altar in metres, correct to two decimal places.
**(i)** Use the rope rule for the diagonal to show that the square built on the diagonal of the old altar has area $128$ square metres.

answer.model_answer_md: By the rope rule, the square on the diagonal equals the squares on the two sides together: $8^2 + 8^2 = 64 + 64 = 128$ square metres. So the square built on the diagonal has area $128$ square metres, double the old altar.

children.solution_md: Add the squares on the two sides.

marking_scheme.step: Square on the diagonal has area 128, double the old

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** A Sulba Sutra rule gives $\sqrt{2} \approx \dfrac{577}{408}$. Use it to find the diagonal of the old altar, correct to two decimal places.

answer.model_answer_md: The diagonal is $8\sqrt{2} \approx 8 \times \dfrac{577}{408} = \dfrac{4616}{408} \approx 11.31$ m.

alternatives.solution_md: Multiply the side by the rule for the square root of 2.

questions.passage_md: Meera, a student in Kolkata, constructs an equilateral triangle $ABC$ on a segment $AB$ of length $9$ cm with a ruler and a compass, as in Euclid's Proposition $1$.

children.stem_md: Drawing the circle with centre $A$ and radius $9$ cm is justified by
children.solution_md: A circle with any centre and any radius is allowed by Postulate $3$. Postulate $1$ joins two points, Postulate $2$ extends a segment, and Postulate $4$ is about right angles.

children.stem_md: Find the perimeter of the triangle $ABC$ in centimetres.
children.solution_md: All three sides are $9$ cm, so the perimeter is $3 \times 9 = 27$ cm.

children.stem_md: **(i)** Explain why $AC = BC$, naming the axiom used.

answer.model_answer_md: $C$ lies on the circle with centre $A$ and radius $AB = 9$ cm, so $AC = AB = 9$ cm. It also lies on the circle with centre $B$ and radius $AB$, so $BC = AB = 9$ cm. Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another (common notion $1$), so $AC = BC$.

children.solution_md: Radii of the two circles, then common notion 1.

marking_scheme.step: AC = AB and BC = AB as radii

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** Meera also draws an equilateral triangle $ABD$ on the other side of $AB$. Find the perimeter of the figure $ACBD$ and name the figure.

answer.model_answer_md: The sides $AC$, $CB$, $BD$ and $DA$ are all $9$ cm, so the perimeter is $4 \times 9 = 36$ cm. A figure with four equal sides is a rhombus.
